items.title: No trustworthy reference standard for alert accuracy
items.whyItMatters: Panels disagree and hindsight moves them towards the known outcome (claim c2), so sensitivity and specificity would be biased.
items.opportunity: Evaluate the checklist as a procedure change with time to decision as the primary outcome.

items.title: Contamination between checklist and usual validation
items.whyItMatters: The same six epidemiologists would validate both arms and carry the checklist over, as reported in the retrieved comparison (claim c1).
items.opportunity: Randomise duty days so that only one procedure is used on any day (claim c3).

items.title: Missed events are too rare to compare statistically
items.whyItMatters: With about four percent true alerts (claim c4), each arm will see fewer than 20 real events in six months.
items.opportunity: Review every dismissed true event case by case with a pre-specified safety rule.

items.title: Small-count signals from care homes and rural areas
items.whyItMatters: A checklist that favours large counts could dismiss small clusters where vulnerable people live (claim c5).
items.opportunity: Include an explicit care home and small-area check and report dismissals by setting.

items.title: Two undated reports claim benefit without data
items.whyItMatters: A triage summary and a workshop report cannot be rated and should not be cited as support.
items.opportunity: Leave them unrated; request data from the national centre only if needed.

errorsFound: The need frames the checklist as a test; it is a change in procedure, and its accuracy cannot be estimated without a reference standard that hindsight does not bias.
reevaluation: The gaps favour a randomised comparison of procedures with day-level allocation, time to decision as the primary outcome and case review of missed events.
summary: Five gaps; the weak reference standard and contamination are high severity.
